sceneHappening: Paul skips the thanks and defends the one true gospel, which came to him by revelation from Christ
summary: Paul, "an apostle, not from men, neither through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead," and all the brothers with him, write to the churches of Galatia: grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, "who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us out of this present evil age." Where a letter would normally give thanks, Paul says, "I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different good news; which is not another good news. Only there are some who trouble you, and want to pervert the Good News of Christ." Even if an angel from heaven should preach anything else, "let him be cursed," and he says it twice. Is he now trying to win the approval of people? "If I were still pleasing men, I wouldn't be a servant of Christ." He insists the gospel he preached was not man's: he didn't receive it from a human source, "but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ." He reminds them of his former life in Judaism, how he persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it, advancing beyond many of his own age in zeal for the traditions of his ancestors. But when God, who set him apart from his mother's womb and called him by grace, was pleased to reveal his Son in him so that he might preach him among the Gentiles, he did not confer with flesh and blood or go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before him, but went to Arabia and returned to Damascus. Then, after three years, he went up to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas and stayed fifteen days; he saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother. ("I assure you, before God, that I am not lying.") Then he went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia, still unknown by face to the churches of Judea, who only heard that the former persecutor was now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy, "and they glorified God in me."
whySettingMatters: Letters in Paul's day usually opened with a prayer of thanks, and the missing thanksgiving is the first sign of how serious things are. The "different gospel" being offered in Galatia seems to have come from other Jewish-Christian teachers who said Gentile believers needed circumcision and the law of Moses to be full members of God's people. Paul never names them (the label "Judaizers" is later), and we only hear his side. To answer the charge that he is a second-hand apostle, he tells his own story in detail. That story overlaps with Acts 9 but does not match it in every detail; for example, Acts does not mention Arabia, and the visits to Jerusalem are counted differently in Galatians and Acts, which is one reason for the debates about the letter's date. "Arabia" probably means the Nabatean kingdom east and south of Damascus. His language about being set apart from his mother's womb echoes the calls of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and the Servant (Isaiah 49:1). "Cursed" translates the Greek anathema, and the word is the same one used in 1 Corinthians 16:22.

questions: Paul skips the usual thanks and goes straight to astonishment. What does that tell us about the stakes?
Paul says the gospel he preaches came by revelation of Jesus Christ and not from people. Why does the source of the message matter?
Paul tells a story that includes his own violent past. Why is his history part of his argument?
"If I were still trying to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ." How do you hold together caring for people and refusing to bend the message?
